cheatsheet:
**Starting and waiting** (`<pthread.h>`, compile with `-pthread`)
`pthread_t t; pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, &job);` · `void *work(void *arg) { Job *job = arg; ... return NULL; }` · `pthread_join(t, NULL);`

**Shared data**
Threads share globals and memory. Read a thread's results only after joining it.

**Races**
`x++` from several threads loses updates. Guard it: `pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;` · `pthread_mutex_lock(&lock); x++; pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);`

**Splitting work**
`base = n / D, extra = n % D`: the first `extra` drones get one more · some may get none

**Fast and safe**
Add into a local variable, lock once at the end, or give each thread its own result slot.

lessons.title: Threads: many drones, one program
lessons.concept:
A **thread** is a second line of work inside the same program. It runs at the same time as main and shares the same global variables and memory, unlike a forked child.

`pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, &job)` starts `work(&job)` on a new thread. The function takes and returns a `void *`, so you pass it a pointer to whatever it needs.

`pthread_join(t, NULL)` waits for that thread to finish. Only read its results after the join; before that, it may still be working.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: Each drone adds up its own 250 numbers of 1–1000. The printing happens after each join, so it's always in drone order.

options: Waits until thread t has finished
drills.answer: Waits until thread t has finished
drills.explain: Join is how main knows the thread's results are ready.

drills.prompt: Fill the blanks to run `work` on a thread and wait for it.
drills.explain: Pass the function itself (no brackets) to pthread_create, and the thread's handle to pthread_join.

drills.prompt: A drone should add up 1 to n on its own thread. The program crashes. Look closely at how the thread is started, then fix it.
drills.explain: `work(&job)` **calls** work right there in main, and its NULL result is handed over as the function to run, so the new thread jumps to address 0. Pass `work` and `&job` separately.

drills.prompt: Two drones share the job: one adds up the **even** numbers, the other the **odd** ones. Write `add_matching` (it gets a `Job *`) and start both drones on it, then print `even E odd O`.
drills.explain: Both threads read the same array, which is fine: nobody changes it. Each writes only to its own Job, so they never get in each other's way. Use `% 2 != 0` for odd, because -3 % 2 is -1, not 1.

lessons.title: Race conditions and mutexes
lessons.concept:
`delivered++` looks like one step, but it's three: read the value, add 1, write it back. Two threads can both read 41, both write 42, and one delivery vanishes. On the judge, four threads doing 100000 unprotected `++` each ended up near **175000**, not 400000, and a different number every run. That's a **race condition**.

A **mutex** is a lock only one thread can hold. `pthread_mutex_lock(&lock)` waits until it's free and takes it; `pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock)` gives it back. Code between the two runs one thread at a time.

Make one with `pthread_mutex_t lock = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;` and guard **every** access to the shared variable.

predict.prompt: Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.explain: With the lock, none of the 4 × 100000 increments can collide, so none are lost.

drills.prompt: Why isn't `count++` safe when several threads do it at once?
options: It's really read, add, write: two threads can read the same old value and one update is lost
++ only works on the main thread
It makes the program run out of memory
drills.answer: It's really read, add, write: two threads can read the same old value and one update is lost
drills.explain: The steps from different threads can interleave in any order.

drills.prompt: Four drones each make `trips` deliveries, but the total keeps coming out short, and different every run. There's already a mutex declared. Use it.
drills.explain: Lock before the increment and unlock right after, so only one drone touches `delivered` at a time.

drills.prompt: A thread locks the mutex and returns without unlocking it. What happens to the other threads?
options: They wait for the lock forever, so the program hangs (the judge reports a timeout)
The lock opens itself when the thread ends
drills.answer: They wait for the lock forever, so the program hangs (the judge reports a timeout)
drills.explain: Every lock needs its unlock on every path out, including early returns.

drills.prompt: Order and indent the lines into a delivery thread that never loses a count.
drills.explain: Lock, change the shared value, unlock: the smallest possible locked region.

lessons.title: Splitting the work fairly
lessons.concept:
To share n items among D drones, give each `n / D`, and hand the leftover `n % D` out one each to the first drones. For 10 items and 3 drones that's 4, 3, 3. Some drones may get **nothing** when n is small, and that has to work too.

Locking for every single addition is slow: the drones spend their time queueing for the lock. Better: each drone adds into its own **local** variable, then locks **once** to add its result to the shared total.

Even better, when you can: give each drone its own result slot, and let main combine them after joining. No lock needed at all.

predict.prompt: It's fed `10`. Before you run it: type what it prints.
predict.answer:
drone 0: 1-4
drone 1: 5-7
drone 2: 8-10
sum of squares 1..10 = 385
predict.explain: 10 / 3 is 3 with 1 left over, so drone 0 gets an extra number. 1 + 4 + 9 + … + 100 = 385.

drills.prompt: With the example's rule, how are 1–11 split across 3 drones?
drills.code: long base = n / DRONES, extra = n % DRONES;
drills.explain: 11 / 3 is 3 with 2 left over, so the first two drones get 4 and the last gets 3.

drills.prompt: Which is faster with 4 drones and 10 million additions?
options: Each drone adds into a local variable, then locks once to add it to the total
No lock at all, it's just addition
drills.answer: Each drone adds into a local variable, then locks once to add it to the total
drills.explain: Locking once per drone instead of once per number removes almost all the waiting, and the answer is still exact.

drills.prompt: Four drones find the biggest value: split the n numbers (n ≥ 1, maybe fewer than 4!) into slices, let each drone find the max of its slice, then combine in main and print `max M`. The `Slice` struct is ready.
drills.explain: Each drone writes only its own Slice, so no lock is needed. The traps: an empty slice has no max at all (skip it when combining), and starting from 0 breaks all-negative input.

checkpoint.prompt: After `pthread_create(&t, NULL, work, &job);`, when does `work` run?
options: Straight away, at the same time as main
checkpoint.answer: Straight away, at the same time as main
checkpoint.explain: The thread starts immediately; join just waits for it to end.

checkpoint.prompt: What does a program using threads need?
options: `#include <pthread.h>`, and the `-pthread` flag when compiling (the judge adds it here)
checkpoint.answer: `#include <pthread.h>`, and the `-pthread` flag when compiling (the judge adds it here)
checkpoint.explain: Without -pthread the program fails to link: *undefined reference to pthread_create*.
Each thread triples a different variable (6 and 15), and main reads them after both joins.

checkpoint.prompt: Two threads each do `count++` a million times with no lock. What's the final count?
options: Usually less than 2000000, and different every run
checkpoint.answer: Usually less than 2000000, and different every run
checkpoint.explain: Lost updates from the race. A mutex (or separate counters) fixes it.

checkpoint.prompt: What does `pthread_mutex_lock(&lock)` do if another thread already holds the lock?
options: Waits until it's unlocked, then takes it
Unlocks it for the other thread
checkpoint.answer: Waits until it's unlocked, then takes it
checkpoint.explain: That waiting is what keeps the protected code one-at-a-time.
